title: Phosphorus in Plants: What It Does and When Your Crop Needs It
metaTitle: Phosphorus in Plants: Role, Signs and When to Apply
metaDescription: Phosphorus in plants carries energy, builds roots and sets the grain. See when palay, mais and gulay need it most, and why it must go in early.
excerpt: Phosphorus in plants is the energy nutrient. It carries the energy every cell runs on, builds new roots, and later moves into the seed and the grain. A crop needs it most when it is young, which is why phosphorus goes in at planting and not as a late topdress. Here is what it does, when each crop needs it, and why it often sits in the soil out of reach.

heroImage.alt: Older leaves turning purple red: phosphorus in plants running short

blocks.text:
Phosphorus is part of ATP, the molecule that carries energy from where the leaves make it to where the plant spends it. Every time a cell divides, a root grows or a sugar moves, phosphorus is in the middle of it. It is also part of DNA and of the membranes around every cell.

So phosphorus decides how fast a young crop gets going. A seedling with enough of it roots deep and fast, tillers early and flowers on time. Later, phosphorus moves into the seed and the grain, which is why a crop short of it fills poorly and matures late.
A building block and an energy carrier

Phosphorus is a building block. It becomes part of the plant body, in its genes, its cell walls and its seeds, and the harvest takes it away. A ton of palay grain carries off roughly 2 to 3 kilograms of phosphorus, which is much less than nitrogen, but it has to be replaced all the same.

Unlike nitrogen, phosphorus does not wash away easily. The trouble is the reverse: it binds so tightly to the soil that the crop reaches only a small part of what is there. That is why where and when you place it matters as much as how much.

blocks.caption: Phosphorus in short
rows: The old, lower leaves, often purple

blocks.text:
Phosphorus moves inside the plant, so a shortage also starts on the older leaves. But it seldom yellows them the way nitrogen does. Instead the plant stays small and stiff, the leaves turn dark green, and in corn, tomato and many young plants the older leaves turn purple or reddish.

In palay the sign is fewer tillers and late, uneven maturity rather than a color. See [phosphorus deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/phosphorus-deficiency) for the signs crop by crop.
When phosphorus in plants is most critical

Phosphorus matters most at the start. Young roots need it the day they form, and a crop that runs short in its first weeks rarely catches up, even if phosphorus comes later. So it belongs in the soil at planting or transplanting, worked in near the roots.

DAT means days after transplanting, DAS days after sowing in the field, and DAP days after planting. The days are the usual ones for a typical variety, so a long or short variety moves them a little. Timing phosphorus in plants to these windows gets more harvest from the same bags. Our guide to [fertilizer timing by growth stage](/blog/fertilizer-timing-by-growth-stage) puts them together for a whole season.

blocks.text: What keeps phosphorus from the crop

Most soils hold far more phosphorus than any crop needs, but little of it is in a form the roots can take. On acid soil it locks up with iron and aluminum. On alkaline and limy soil it locks up with calcium. It is most available when the soil pH sits near 6 to 7.

Cold, waterlogged or compacted soil also slows phosphorus uptake, because roots grow little there. Organic matter helps, and so does placing the fertilizer close to the roots instead of spreading it thinly over the surface. In a flooded paddy, phosphorus becomes easier to take up as the soil softens, which is one reason rice suffers less from it than upland crops.

Phosphorus comes in the fertilizers you use at planting. Ammonium phosphate is the usual choice for palay and mais, with complete fertilizer when the soil also needs potassium. See our guides to [16 20 0 fertilizer](/blog/16-20-0-fertilizer) and [complete fertilizer](/blog/complete-fertilizer-14-14-14).

blocks.title: Too much phosphorus locks up zinc
blocks.text: Phosphorus piled on season after season builds up in the soil and makes zinc and iron harder for the crop to take. If a soil test already shows plenty, put the money into the nutrient that is short instead.

blocks.title: Check that phosphorus is in before the roots need it
blocks.text: Put your fertilizers on your crop's calendar in anee.io and the [Coverage Planner](/features/residual-effect-calendar) shows, day by day, whether phosphorus reaches the stages that need it, and where it runs out. Free to start.

items.q: Should phosphorus go in at planting or later?
items.a: At planting. Young roots need it first, and phosphorus moves very little in the soil, so it has to be close to the roots from the start. A late phosphorus topdress does little for the yield.

items.q: Why are my corn leaves purple?
items.a: Purple older leaves on young corn often mean a phosphorus shortage, most of all on cold, wet or acid soil. Some hybrids turn purple for a few days on their own, so check whether the plants are also small and slow.
Yes. Phosphorus is a primary macronutrient, with nitrogen and potassium, though crops take less of it than of the other two.
On acid soil, yes. Raising the pH toward 6 frees phosphorus that was locked with iron and aluminum. On alkaline soil lime makes it worse.
